title: GDP base-year revision (2015) and the contested back-series
whatChanged: CSO moved the GDP base year from 2004-05 to 2011-12 in January 2015, adopting GVA and SNA 2008 methodology with MCA-21 corporate data. FY2013-14 growth reads 4.7% on the old base but 6.9% on the new. Two conflicting back-series followed in 2018: the NSC Mundle committee version (higher UPA growth, double-digit peaks) and the CSO/NITI Aayog version (lower UPA growth). Arvind Subramanian (2019) argued 2011-17 growth was overstated by ~2.5pp.
bridgeNote: No accepted reconciliation. Instrument policy: carry both series with a visible seam; never splice.

competingAccounts.position: Back-series lowers UPA-era growth; official position
Back-series shows higher UPA growth incl. double-digit years; shelved as 'experimental'
Post-2011 growth overstated ~2.5pp; actual ~4.5% vs official ~7% for 2011-17
Subramanian critique cherry-picked, not statistically robust

title: EUS to PLFS employment survey transition
whatChanged: NSSO Employment-Unemployment Survey (quinquennial, last round 2011-12) replaced by Periodic Labour Force Survey from 2017-18, with changed sampling design and stratification. Pre/post employment comparisons are methodologically contested; no official bridge estimates exist.

title: Withheld 2017-18 Consumer Expenditure Survey
whatChanged: The NSS 2017-18 Household Consumer Expenditure Survey was not released after leaked results indicated declining rural consumption; the government cited data-quality issues. Result: no official consumption-based poverty estimate after 2011-12 until the 2022-23 HCES (itself on a changed methodology).
bridgeNote: 2022-23 HCES uses a modified questionnaire and imputation approach; not comparable with 2011-12 without contested adjustments.

title: Census 2021 not conducted
whatChanged: The decennial census due 2021 was postponed (COVID cited) and has not been conducted as of the project's last update. Every per-capita and rate-based indicator after 2011 rests on population projections, with error compounding over time.

title: WPI-to-CPI inflation regime change
whatChanged: Headline inflation reference shifted from WPI to CPI (combined) around 2013-14; formal CPI inflation targeting (4% +/-2%) adopted 2016 via amended RBI Act. Long-run inflation narratives spanning the change must state which index they use.
bridgeNote: Both indices continue to be published; the break is interpretive, not a data gap.

title: Off-budget borrowing and fiscal accounting
whatChanged: Off-budget devices (FCI food-subsidy bonds, NSSF loans to public entities) understate the headline fiscal deficit in both eras. CAG flagged the practice; a partial clean-up brought FCI dues on-budget in FY2020-21, creating a one-year spike that is an accounting artefact, not a spending surge.
bridgeNote: CAG and budget documents allow partial reconstruction of extended deficit measures.
notes: Scope extended to banking: the Oct 2017 recapitalisation used ~₹1.35 lakh crore of recap bonds, which are the same off-budget device this record describes.

title: NCRB reporting changes and communal-violence data gaps
whatChanged: NCRB definitional and tabulation changes across editions, plus discontinuation/re-housing of communal-violence reporting between MHA and NCRB, complicate crime and communal-incident trend analysis across 2014.

title: Contested governance indices (RSF, Freedom House, V-Dem)
whatChanged: Third-party democracy/press indices carry their own methodology disputes and periodic recalibrations. Baseline readings circa 2014: RSF rank ~140 (score ~40.3); Freedom House 'Free' (downgrade to 'Partly Free' came 2021); V-Dem liberal-democracy scores higher pre-2014. Recorded as readings, not settled facts; the government contests their methods.

sources.name: RSF World Press Freedom Index archive

title: Peer-country GDP rebasings and WDI vintage drift
whatChanged: Comparator countries revised their own national accounts inside the study window: Vietnam's 2021 rebasing lifted GDP levels ~25%; Bangladesh rebased to 2015-16 with a similar upward level shift. World Bank WDI back-propagates these, so the same query on different dates returns different histories. The peer panel must be pinned to a single WDI vintage, recorded in every series' source.vintage field.
bridgeNote: Pin one WDI vintage for the whole panel; re-pull the entire panel, never one country, when refreshing.
notes: Scoped to 'all': this is a methodological property of every World Bank WDI pull, not a macro-specific one — any domain carrying a peer panel inherits it.

title: Third GDP base-year revision to 2022-23 (released 27 February 2026)
whatChanged: MoSPI released a new national accounts series rebased from 2011-12 to 2022-23, adopting double deflation, a Supply-Use Table framework, and new source data (GST returns, PLFS, ASUSE). The revision to recent growth is MIXED, not uniformly upward: FY24 was revised DOWN from 8.2% to 7.2%, while FY25 was revised UP from 6.5% to 7.1%; FY26 is estimated at 7.6%. This changes the SHAPE of the recent trajectory, not just its level — on the 2011-12 base the FY24-to-FY25 move was a 1.7-point deceleration, on the 2022-23 base it is a 0.1-point one. Separately, the revision lowered the LEVEL of nominal GDP by roughly 3-4%, which mechanically raises every ratio-to-GDP in the project without any change in underlying activity.
bridgeNote: Back-series to be spliced at disaggregated level; not yet published. Until it is, FY24 and FY25 have two valid growth figures and every ratio-to-GDP has two valid denominators. Instrument policy: THREE regimes, never one line.

competingAccounts.position: Routine decadal rebasing to a recent normal post-COVID year; methodologically superior (double deflation, SUT, GST-based data)

A rebasing that simultaneously raises growth and lowers the level arrives conveniently; the absence of published Sources and Methods until Aug 2026 makes independent verification impossible in the interim

sources.name: MoSPI Press Note on New Series of GDP Estimates, base 2022-23

notes: Supersedes the project's original two-regime assumption. CLAUDE.md rule 5 must be amended from 'both GDP series' to 'all three regimes'. CORRECTION 2026-07-31: earlier wording of this record generalised the revision as upward, which contradicts its own FY24 figures. Direction is mixed and is now stated per year. The flattening of the FY24-FY25 deceleration is a substantive narrative effect and should be surfaced wherever growth trajectory is discussed. Scoped to 'all': the GDP denominator is inherited by any ratio-to-GDP series in any domain — health and education spending shares trip this as surely as fiscal or trade ratios do.

title: CPI base revision to 2024 (new series from February 2026)
whatChanged: A new CPI series with base year 2024 was introduced, with weights redrawn from the Household Consumption Expenditure Survey and a higher non-food weight. Since food inflation drove most headline breaches in 2020 and 2022-23, a lower food weight mechanically dampens future headline volatility relative to the old basket — meaning post-2026 inflation performance is not directly comparable with the 2014-2025 record on which the inflation-targeting verdict rests.
bridgeNote: Weight-effect decomposition would be needed to compare like with like across the break.
notes: Tier-4 sourcing pending a T1 MoSPI press note pull. Flagged in the open verification queue.

title: IIP and WPI base revisions; new Producer Price Index
whatChanged: IIP rebasing to 2022-23 (due around May 2026), a WPI revision in progress, and a planned Producer Price Index. Industrial-production and wholesale-price series will break at these points.

title: Fiscal anchor changes from deficit to debt (from FY2026-27)
whatChanged: From FY27 the Centre shifts its operational fiscal anchor from the annual fiscal-deficit ratio to a debt-to-GDP target (central debt ~56.1% in FY26, glide to 50%±1% by FY31). Fiscal performance before and after FY27 is therefore benchmarked against different objectives. Compounding: P-10 lowered the GDP denominator by 3-4%, which raises measured debt/GDP without any change in borrowing.
bridgeNote: Both measures remain computable; the break is in what counts as success, not in the data.

title: World Bank WDI fiscal-year labelling for India versus calendar years for peers
whatChanged: WDI labels India's fiscal-year observations by the starting calendar year, so WDI '2014' for India corresponds to FY2014-15 (Apr 2014-Mar 2015), while '2014' for Bangladesh, Vietnam, Indonesia and China is a different period basis. Peer comparisons drawn straight from WDI therefore compare India's FY with peers' CY, offset by up to nine months — material when a shock (2020 COVID, 2022 commodity spike) lands mid-year. This also explains the apparent conflict between the Phase 1 exports figure (25.4% of GDP, FY2013-14, T1) and WDI's 22.97% for '2014': they are different periods, not contradictory sources.
bridgeNote: State the period basis on every peer chart; never present an India WDI year and a peer WDI year as the same period without the offset noted. VERIFY the WDI India labelling convention against WDI documentation before relying on this record.
notes: Discovered while reconciling Phase 1 and Phase 2 export figures. Convention stated from general knowledge — flagged for primary verification. Scoped to 'all': this is a methodological property of every World Bank WDI pull, not a macro-specific one — any domain carrying a peer panel inherits it.

title: Asset Quality Review recognition break (2015-16)
whatChanged: The RBI's Asset Quality Review forced uniform recognition of stressed accounts previously evergreened through Corporate Debt Restructuring, and withdrew special dispensations for restructured loans. Reported NPA ratios rose steeply as a result of RECOGNITION, not of deterioration: PSB gross NPAs went from 4.97% (Mar 2015) to a peak of 14.58% (Mar 2018). Pre-2015 NPA figures are therefore not comparable with post-AQR figures — the 4.4% recorded at the 2014 handover describes a reporting regime, not an asset quality.
bridgeNote: No official restatement of pre-AQR figures exists. Any chart spanning 2015-16 must mark the break; the rise is not a deterioration event.

competingAccounts.position: Recognition was necessary and overdue; delay would have compounded the eventual cost
Execution was too abrupt and precipitated a credit squeeze — PCA-bank loan books shrank ~11% FY15-FY18, contributing to the pre-COVID slowdown

sources.name: PIB, GNPA of PSBs declined from the peak of 14.58%

notes: Replaces an incorrect reference to P-06 (off-budget borrowing) carried in the phase-1 seed data.

title: COVID-era regulatory forbearance suppressing reported NPAs
whatChanged: The March-August 2020 loan moratorium, the Supreme Court-ordered asset classification standstill, and successive restructuring windows suppressed reported NPA figures through FY2020-21 and FY2021-22. Reported ratios for those years understate underlying stress, and the subsequent decline partly reflects forbearance unwinding rather than a clean trajectory.

title: Write-offs and denominator growth flattering the headline NPA ratio
whatChanged: The fall in the gross NPA ratio from its 2018 peak is driven by three distinct mechanisms that the headline number does not separate: genuine recoveries and upgrades (RBI attributes ~42.8% of the FY2024-25 reduction to these), write-offs (₹16,61,310 crore cumulative April 2014-September 2024, of which only ₹2,69,795 crore — about 16% — was recovered), and rapid credit growth expanding the denominator (domestic credit rose from ₹66.91 to ₹181.34 lakh crore, 2015-2025). The ratio improvement is real but overstates the extent of genuine cleanup.
bridgeNote: Adjusted series = (gross NPA amount + cumulative write-offs) / gross advances, all on the SAME bank population and the SAME reporting basis. REQUIRES: scb-gross-npa-amount, scb-gross-advances, and a cumulative write-off series for the identical population. Currently renderable ONLY for SCB domestic operations at FY2013-14, FY2017-18 and FY2024-25 — the three sourced points. NOT renderable for PSBs: write-offs are all-SCB, so applying them to a PSB ratio mixes populations and describes neither group. NOT renderable as a continuous annual line until an annual advances series is pinned from RBI Trend & Progress. Do not substitute 'domestic credit' for gross advances.

competingAccounts.position: A write-off is an accounting measure that does not extinguish borrower liability; recovery efforts continue on written-off accounts
Recovery on written-off accounts runs at roughly 13-18% in practice, so the distinction is largely notional for the bulk of the amount; depositors and taxpayers absorbed the loss

sources.name: PIB, Building Trust: Strengthening India's banking sector

notes: The single most consequential interpretive issue in the banking domain. Write-off totals derive from RBI RTI responses reported through journalism; the government disputes the interpretation, not the figures.

title: Domestic-operations versus global-operations reporting basis
whatChanged: Indian NPA statistics are published on two bases and official sources mix them without always labelling which is in use. The frequently quoted PSB peak of 14.58% (March 2018) is on the global-operations basis; the scheduled-commercial-bank figure for the same period on domestic operations is 11.46%. Comparing a figure on one basis with a figure on the other produces spurious movements of two to three percentage points.
bridgeNote: Tag every NPA point with its basis. Never compare across bases without conversion.

sources.name: PIB, SCB gross NPAs for domestic operations

title: Risk-weight changes on unsecured retail and NBFC lending (Nov 2023, partial rollback Feb 2025)
whatChanged: In November 2023 the RBI raised risk weights on unsecured consumer credit from 100% to 125% and added 25 percentage points to bank lending to NBFCs. In February 2025 it partially rolled this back — bank-to-NBFC weights restored effective 1 April 2025 and the microfinance consumer-credit weight cut back to 100% — while retaining 125% on unsecured retail. Capital ratios and unsecured-credit growth series are not comparable across FY2024 to FY2026 without accounting for these changes.

title: RBI fraud reporting: date of occurrence versus date of detection
whatChanged: The RBI is reported to have changed the basis of its fraud statistics from date of detection to date of occurrence, which materially changes year-on-year fraud totals and reassigns large historical frauds to earlier years. Any fraud time series spanning the change is not comparable.
bridgeNote: The change is asserted across multiple secondary sources but the primary RBI circular and its effective date have NOT been located. Do not publish any fraud time series until this is pinned.

sources.name: Secondary reporting, pending primary RBI notification

notes: Highest-priority verification item from this cycle. This record is provisional.

title: Expected Credit Loss provisioning transition (from 1 April 2027)
whatChanged: RBI final directions issued 27 April 2026 mandate a shift from incurred-loss to expected-credit-loss provisioning effective 1 April 2027, with a glide path to March 2031. Estimated one-time capital impact is around 60-70 basis points system-wide, larger for banks with heavy unsecured or microfinance exposure. Provisioning coverage and reported asset-quality figures after FY2027 will not be directly comparable with prior years.
bridgeNote: A forward-dated break. Set a re-baselining trigger for FY2027-28 data.

title: Evidence base shifts from independent survey to scheme MIS
whatChanged: From 2014 onward the primary evidence for welfare performance shifted from independent statistical surveys (NSSO/NSS rounds) toward scheme management information systems and dashboards. MIS records an OUTPUT — a connection issued, a toilet built, a card created, a house sanctioned — not sustained use. Every coverage figure sourced from MIS is therefore an upper bound on the outcome it is cited to demonstrate, and the wedge is largest exactly where the welfare payoff depends on behaviour change.
bridgeNote: Pair every MIS figure with the best independent estimate where one exists: CAG refill data for Ujjwala, r.i.c.e. SQUAT for sanitation, the 2024 Functionality Assessment for JJM, claims-paid for PM-JAY. Where no independent estimate exists, label the figure as administrative and unverified. BOTH SIDES of every pair carry this record: the usage-side series exists precisely to measure the wedge, so a reader asking what a functionality or admissions figure rests on must reach it. Where a coverage series has no usage counterpart, the record must state that none exists rather than rendering alone — pmay-g-completed pairs the housing cascade, but occupancy remains unmeasured.

sources.name: PIB, India's DBT: Boosting Welfare Efficiency

notes: The organising measurement problem of the welfare domain. Every scheme record in this phase references it. Scope includes infrastructure: Jal Jeevan is filed there and is one of the clearest MIS-versus-survey cases in the dataset. Scope extended to employment: EPFO net payroll additions and e-Shram registrations are registration counts standing in for outcomes, the same shape this record describes.

title: HCES 2022-23 methodology change breaks consumption comparability
whatChanged: The Household Consumption Expenditure Survey 2022-23 and 2023-24 adopted a Modified Mixed Recall Period, a three-visit design, and imputation of items received free under government schemes. Imputing scheme transfers raises measured consumption by construction, and none of it is comparable with the 2011-12 round. Combined with the withheld 2017-18 survey (P-03), there is no comparable consumption series across the entire period under study.
bridgeNote: No official bridge. Derived poverty estimates diverge widely — NITI suggesting 5% or less, SBI Research 4-7%, Rangarajan-line reconstruction ~8.6%. Report the RANGE, never a point estimate. The India Forum notes the 2022-23 design under-samples poor households and recommends a dedicated bridge survey.

competingAccounts.position: Poverty has fallen to around 5% or less on the new data
Rangarajan-line reconstruction gives ~8.6% for 2022-23; the survey under-samples the poor and imputation inflates consumption

title: ODF, ODF-Plus and ODF-Plus Model are successive non-identical definitions
whatChanged: Rural India was declared Open Defecation Free in October 2019, after which ODF-Plus and ODF-Plus Model were introduced as further tiers. Each redefines the threshold, so apparent progress across the sequence partly reflects definitional change rather than behavioural change. The underlying ODF declaration is itself contested: the r.i.c.e. SQUAT panel found open defecation among people over two in Bihar, MP, Rajasthan and UP fell from 70% (2014) to 44% (2018), and that 23% of latrine-owners still defecated in the open — unchanged from 2014.

competingAccounts.position: 93.1% of rural households had toilets and 96.5% of those with access used them
44% of people over two still defecating in the open in four large north-Indian states; 23% of latrine-owners unchanged since 2014

notes: Questionnaire design accounts for part of the divergence: grouped household questions structurally understate open defecation relative to person-by-person questions.

title: JJM certification measures infrastructure, not water delivered
whatChanged: A 'certified Har Ghar Jal village' under Jal Jeevan Mission records tap connections installed, not water delivered. The Ministry's own 2024 Functionality Assessment across 19,812 certified villages found 98% of households had a tap but only about 76% received water meeting Mission standards and about 83% the minimum quantity norm.
bridgeNote: The 2024 Functionality Assessment quantifies the wedge directly — carry both series and show the gap.

title: MPI circularity: the poverty measure is built from the scheme outputs it is used to validate
whatChanged: In the absence of consumption-based poverty estimates, the Multidimensional Poverty Index became the headline poverty measure. Its indicators include cooking fuel, sanitation, housing, drinking water and bank accounts — which are precisely the outputs of Ujjwala, Swachh Bharat, PMAY, Jal Jeevan and Jan Dhan. Scheme delivery therefore improves the poverty measure mechanically, regardless of whether the output converted into sustained use. NITI Aayog's claim that 24.82 crore people exited multidimensional poverty between 2013-14 and 2022-23 cannot be cited as independent confirmation that those schemes worked.
bridgeNote: State the circularity explicitly wherever the 24.82 crore figure appears. A NITI member has acknowledged that a scheme targets each of the 12 MPI indicators.

competingAccounts.position: 24.82 crore exited multidimensional poverty; headcount fell 29.17% to 11.28%
Improvement is partly definitional; MPI indicators are scheme outputs whose usage is separately contested

title: PM-JAY card creation is an eligibility token, not utilisation
whatChanged: Ayushman Bharat reports three numbers that diverge by an order of magnitude: cards created (24-30+ crore), hospital admissions authorised (12.69 crore by June 2026), and claims paid (over ₹1.92 lakh crore). A card confers eligibility and does not evidence use. The 2023 CAG performance audit additionally found large-scale database integrity failures, including roughly 7.5 lakh beneficiaries linked to a single mobile number.
bridgeNote: Use admissions authorised and claims paid as the utilisation measures; never cite cards as coverage achieved.

competingAccounts.position: Database integrity failures including duplicate mobile numbers, payments for deceased patients, and simultaneous multi-hospital admissions
PM-JAY is entitlement-based not enrolment-based, so mobile numbers do not determine eligibility

title: ABPS and NMMS in MGNREGA suppress recorded demand
whatChanged: The Aadhaar-Based Payment System was made compulsory for MGNREGA from January 2024 after repeated extensions, and the National Mobile Monitoring System app changed attendance recording. Approximately 1.46 crore workers were net-deleted from job cards in FY2023-24. Because MGNREGA is demand-driven, administrative exclusion registers in the data as reduced demand rather than as rationing — the series cannot distinguish the two.
bridgeNote: LibTech India tracks payment delays and deletions independently. In FY2024-25 registrations rose 8.6% while employment delivery fell 7.1% — the divergence is the signature of rationing rather than falling need.

title: Global Hunger Index methodology dispute
whatChanged: India ranked 105 of 127 in the 2024 Global Hunger Index with a score of 27.3 ('serious'), and its child wasting rate of 18.7% is the highest of any country in the index. The Government of India has formally rejected the methodology since 2021, arguing three of four indicators are child-specific and the undernourishment indicator rests on a small opinion poll, and citing its own Poshan Tracker showing child wasting consistently below 7.2%.
bridgeNote: Child wasting is the crux: GHI 18.7% versus Poshan Tracker under 7.2%. The two cannot currently be reconciled and neither should be presented as settled.

competingAccounts.position: Rank 105/127, score 27.3, child wasting 18.7% — the highest in the index
Methodology is flawed: three of four indicators are child-specific, undernourishment rests on a ~3,000-person poll, and Poshan Tracker shows wasting below 7.2%

title: National highway network growth is mostly reclassification, not construction
whatChanged: The NH network grew from 91,287 km (March 2014) to about 146,342 km (mid-2025), routinely cited as a 60% expansion. But MoRTH's own factsheet states roughly 54,004 km of state roads were NOTIFIED as national highways since April 2014. Since the network grew about 55,000 km, the overwhelming majority of the headline expansion is administrative reclassification of existing roads, not new building. The honest output metrics are kilometres built per day (11.6 in FY2013-14, peaking at 37 in FY2020-21) and four-lane-plus length (18,278 to 45,947 km), both of which represent real construction.
bridgeNote: Use nh-construction-pace and nh-four-lane as the build metrics. Never present nh-network-length growth as construction. If MoRTH begins publishing greenfield-only kilometres, substitute that series.
notes: The single most consequential measurement finding in the infrastructure domain.

title: Four-laning of existing highways counts as construction kilometres
whatChanged: MoRTH's construction figures count the widening of existing carriageways alongside genuinely new alignment, so 'kilometres constructed' conflates capacity upgrade with network extension. Both are real work, but they are different things and the series does not separate them.
bridgeNote: Greenfield corridor length is reported separately for expressways but not for the general NH programme.

title: Village electrification and household electrification are different thresholds
whatChanged: Under DDUGJY a village counted as electrified if 10% of its households plus public buildings had a connection — a very low bar, and the basis on which village electrification was declared complete in April 2018. Saubhagya (2017-2019) then connected about 2.86 crore households to claim near-universal HOUSEHOLD access. The shift is a genuine tightening of the standard, but neither threshold measures electricity SUPPLIED: 'electrified' means connected, and around 53% of villages received under 12 hours a day of domestic supply as of 2019.
bridgeNote: No continuous national series of household supply-hours exists — see the declared absence on household-electrification.

title: Railway Budget merged into the Union Budget (2017)
whatChanged: The separate Railway Budget, presented annually since 1924, was merged into the Union Budget from 2017-18, concurrent with the Plan/Non-Plan to capital/revenue reclassification. The railway finance series breaks at that point and pre- and post-merger figures are not directly comparable.

title: Railway punctuality suspended during COVID; accident classification is selective
whatChanged: Punctuality reporting was suspended during the COVID period, leaving a gap in the series. Separately, the headline safety metric counts CONSEQUENTIAL accidents only — a category that excludes many incidents — so the improvement from 135 (FY2014-15) to 31 (FY2024-25) is real on its own terms but narrower than 'accidents' implies.

title: Logistics Performance Index 2023 methodology change
whatChanged: The World Bank's 2023 LPI edition changed methodology and rounds scores to one decimal, and the country set differs between editions. India's rank trajectory (54 in 2014, 44 in 2018, 38 in 2023) is more robust than the score comparison.

title: Logistics cost rebased from 13-14% to about 8% of GDP by a new methodology
whatChanged: The long-cited figure of 13-14% of GDP for India's logistics cost was replaced by a DPIIT/NCAER study (2023) estimating 7.8-8.9% for FY2021-22 and 7.97% for FY2023-24. This is a NEW METHODOLOGY producing a lower estimate, not a measured fall from the old figure. Presenting the two as a time series would show a halving of logistics costs that did not occur.
bridgeNote: No bridge to the old 13-14% figure exists. Never plot the two on one line. The 13-14% number was itself poorly sourced, so this is a case where the new estimate is probably better AND the apparent improvement is an artefact — both can be true.

competingAccounts.position: 7.97% of GDP for FY2023-24 on a documented methodology; the World Bank endorsed the baseline approach
The old 13-14% figure was never rigorously derived, so the gap between the two measures the change in method, not in cost

sources.name: NCAER report on logistics cost in India

title: BharatNet 'service-ready' means middle-mile fibre, not delivered service
whatChanged: A gram panchayat counts as service-ready when middle-mile fibre reaches it — not when any household or institution receives service. 2,14,904 of 2,22,341 Phase I and II GPs were service-ready by December 2025, but functional last-mile delivery lags substantially. Cost rose from ₹20,000 crore to about ₹1.39 lakh crore and the deadline has been revised more than six times.

title: Airport count includes heliports, waterdromes and reclassified airstrips
whatChanged: The frequently cited rise from 74 operational airports in 2014 to about 160 includes 9 heliports and 2 waterdromes, and counts reactivated or reclassified airstrips as new. A July 2023 Rajya Sabha reply confirmed only about 11 genuinely greenfield airports were built since May 2014.
bridgeNote: Greenfield airport count (~11) is the construction metric; the ~160 figure is an operational-facility count on a broadened definition.

title: PLFS sample redesign of January 2025 breaks the series against itself
whatChanged: From January 2025 the Periodic Labour Force Survey was substantially redesigned: first-stage units rose from 12,800 to 22,692, households per unit from 8 to 12, total sample to about 2.72 lakh households — roughly 2.65 times the previous 1.02 lakh — with a monthly rotational panel introduced in both rural and urban areas, changed stratification using districts as strata where possible, and the annual reference year shifted from July-June to January-December. MoSPI states explicitly that results from January 2025 onward may not be strictly comparable with earlier PLFS rounds.
bridgeNote: A calendar-year back-series to 2022 was reconstructed but is flagged as not strictly comparable. This is the SECOND instrument change inside this domain: EUS to PLFS in 2017-18 (P-02), then PLFS to redesigned PLFS in 2025. The employment series therefore has three regimes, none officially bridged, across a period of twelve years.
notes: Re-baseline the longitudinal dataset at 2025. Do not splice across January 2025.

title: Unpaid family helpers are counted as employed
whatChanged: PLFS classifies unpaid helpers in household enterprises as employed, and counts subsidiary activity of 30 days or more over a 365-day recall. An unemployment rate computed on this definition falls when people are absorbed into unpaid family work, which is the opposite of what a falling unemployment rate is normally taken to mean. The unpaid-helper share rose from about 13.3% of workers in 2018-19 to 17.3% in 2020-21, and the self-employed share to 58.4% by 2023-24, while regular wage employment stayed flat at 21-23%.
bridgeNote: Read the unemployment rate only alongside the status composition — self-employed, unpaid helper, regular wage and casual shares — and alongside agriculture's employment share. Current weekly status unemployment, which uses a seven-day recall, runs materially higher throughout (8.7% in 2017-18 against 6.0% usual status) and is the better measure of open joblessness.

competingAccounts.position: Counting contributing family workers as employed follows international standards and is not an Indian idiosyncrasy
Whatever the convention, a headline rate that falls as unpaid work rises cannot be cited as evidence that jobs were created

title: PLFS and CMIE disagree on the direction of employment change
whatChanged: The official PLFS and the private CMIE Consumer Pyramids Household Survey do not merely differ in level; over 2017-18 to 2021-22 PLFS records employment growth of +4.55% (+88.86 million) while CMIE records minus 0.30% (5.62 million fewer) — opposite signs. PLFS puts unemployment at 3.2% and LFPR at about 60% for 2023-24; CMIE puts unemployment at 7-9% and LFPR near 40% across the same period. The divergence is concentrated almost entirely among women, whose measured work participation in official data is roughly double CMIE's, with no convergence across reference periods.
bridgeNote: No reconciliation exists and none should be manufactured. The instruments answer different questions: PLFS supports statements about participation and status composition; CMIE supports statements about open joblessness among urban, educated and female workers. Carry both series and never present one as the employment picture.

competingAccounts.position: Statutory national survey, large sample, Census-consistent demographics, ILO-standard definitions, public unit-level microdata
High-frequency panel design captures discouraged workers exiting the labour force and intermittent joblessness that an annual recall smooths away
Private and subscription-gated, with a contested sampling frame and implausibly low female participation figures
Its employment definition converts distress and unpaid work into employment, mechanically deflating the unemployment rate

sources.name: Abraham and Shrivastava, Indian Journal of Labour Economics

notes: THE defining measurement dispute of this domain. In every earlier phase measurement problems qualified a finding; here the disagreement IS the finding.

title: EPFO net payroll additions are not a count of new jobs
whatChanged: Net subscriber additions to the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation include members re-joining after a gap and members switching employers, not only first-time entrants, and the series is periodically revised. One analysis of 4.86 crore net additions across FY2020 to FY2023 found roughly 2.27 crore genuinely new payroll entries and about 42 lakh of net formalisation, the remainder being re-joiners and switchers.
bridgeNote: No establishment-level new-hire register exists in India that would allow a true jobs-created series to be constructed.

title: RBI KLEMS estimates employment rather than measuring it
whatChanged: The RBI's India KLEMS database is a total factor productivity framework that takes employment as an INPUT from PLFS and the national accounts. Citing its output — for instance 17.19 crore additional jobs over 2014-24 against 2.9 crore over 2004-14 — as independent evidence of job creation is circular, since the employment figures it reports are derived from the same surveys whose interpretation is in dispute.
notes: Not a fault in KLEMS, which is doing what it was designed to do. The error is in the citation.
